newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Cuban jazz star Rubalcaba makes new home in Florida.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cuban jazz star Rubalcaba makes new home in Florida.

text.p: Cuban pianist Gonzalo Rubalcaba usually raises the temperature with a flamboyant style that has made him one of jazz's most exciting young players.

But he has settled quietly into south Florida, where he hopes some of the political passions that have swirled around him recently will cool down. "I have come here to offer my art. I don't have to explain politics," he told Reuters from his new home in Fort Lauderdale.

While Rubalcaba's move should gain him greater exposure as he aspires to join the ranks of jazz greats, his story also reflects a heated debate in Miami over freedom of expression. Cuban exile groups have hounded artists from Cuba and other Latin American countries who refuse to denounce President Fidel Castro, and when Rubalcaba made his Miami debut at the Gusman Arts Centre in May an angry crowd of exiles spit on and scuffled with concert-goers outside the hall.

The 33-year-old Rubalcaba moved to Florida in November from the Dominican Republic, where he had lived for the last few years, and has kept a low profile since then. He still carries a Cuban passport and has divulged no plans to break with Havana's communist government.

"My relations with Cuba are normal," he said. "They have had no bad reaction to my leaving. Everyone knows my position. I was losing chances to work and develop in Cuba. The social and economic situation is such one has to put a lot of effort dealing with that."
RELAXED CUBAN POLICY ON ARTISTS

Cuba's government has for the past four years allowed artists and performers to live abroad as long as they refrain from criticising it, Max Castro, a senior research associate at the University of Miami's North-South Centre, said.

Realising that it could not support them as in the past, Havana altered its policy to discourage talent from formally defecting, he said. Most of the so-called velvet exiles chose to live in Mexico or elswehere in Latin America.
"The Rubalcaba case is unusual because of the country and place he's chosen," Castro said.

Shortly after the furore over Rubalcaba's Miami appearance, the Centre for Fine Arts withdrew an invitation for Cuban art critic Gerado Mosquera to speak there. Then in July the Centro Vasco restaurant in Little Havana, heart of the Cuban American community, was firebombed after it booked a show by Havana resident Rosita Fornes. It was forced to close in December after business dropped off.

Rubalcaba's move will test the Cuban American community, said Lisa Versace of Miami ArtSave, a group set up last month to guard freedom of expression in the wake of the incidents. "People get very passionate and sometimes push it over the line. But there is a lot of change occuring here," she said.
"Mr. Rubalcaba is here, he lives under the Constitution. He has every right to perform and people have a right to see him."
Rubalcaba has bought a house in neighbouring Fort Lauderdale, away from the passions of Little Havana.
LESS POLITICS IN FORT LAUDERDALE

"I like Miami very much. Cubans have done much to make it what it is. But it is also very political. There are many contradictions. I want a little distance from that," he said. "It is quiet here (in Fort Lauderdale), less politics. I have three small children so it is safe for them."

Rubalcaba has made headlines as much for his virtuosity at the piano as for his unwanted position as a political focus. He was born into a family of musicians in Havana in 1963 and says he was influenced by classical music, traditional Cuban music and jazz piano players ranging from Art Tatum, Bill Evans and Thelonious Monk to modern artists such as Keith Jarret and Herbie Hancock.

After studying at Havana's Amadeo Roldan Conservatory, he toured Europe in 1983 and caused a sensation at his debut at the Montreaux Jazz Festival in 1990. He played extensively in Europe and Japan but, as with other Cuban artists, most of the money he earned abroad went to the Havana government.

He also fell victim to U.S. policy on Cuba and was unable to tour or record in the United States for a long time. His breakthrough international recording, "The Blessing" (1991), was issued by the Japanese arm of the famed Blue Note label.
The late trumpeter Dizzie Gillespie, who visited Havana several times, championed Rubalcaba, but he did not receive permission to play in the United States until 1993.
Now the future looks busy.

Three albums will be released this year and he will play a week at the Blue Note Club in New York this month, followed by concerts in other major U.S. cities in March. Tours of Europe and Japan are also scheduled.
But so far there are no plans for another Miami concert. "I hope there will be a proposal but right now nothing has been offered," he said.
